say.text: You are writing the take-home for Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), one box at a time. Box one: the four classic components.
Which set goes in the box?

choices.label: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, ASD
VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction, RVH
VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, LVH

say.text: Count what the septum, the aorta, the outflow tract and the ventricle each contribute. Only one chamber is overloaded.
Right. The four are a large anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH).
ASD and PDA may accompany TOF, but they are not among the four.
ASD is tempting because it turns up with TOF and gives the pentalogy its fifth member. But it is not one of the four.
PYQs have keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as not part of TOF; current StatPearls lists VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and RVH.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: the four contain no ASD, PDA or LVH.

say.text: LVH is tempting because hypertrophy sounds like the heart's main problem. But it is the right ventricle that hypertrophies.
PYQs have keyed LVH, with ASD and PDA, as not part of TOF.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so a second look is worth it: the fourth component is right ventricular hypertrophy.

say.text: Box two: the arrows. A teammate drafts the causal chain, and you must pick the line that goes in.
Which line is right?

choices.label: RVH is the primary defect, and the thickened muscle narrows the outflow
The obstruction is at the pulmonary valve alone, with nothing below it
Infundibular obstruction sends blood to the aorta, and RVH is secondary

say.text: Ask which comes first in time: the narrowed outflow or the thick muscle. Then ask where the narrowing sits relative to the valve.
Yes. The obstruction is infundibular (sub-pulmonary). With significant obstruction most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the lungs.
The RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures, so it sits at the end of the chain.
Thick muscle narrowing its own outflow is a tidy story, and hypertrophy is in the name of the set. But it is a consequence.
RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures; the obstruction is infundibular.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reread: RVH is the end of the chain, not the start.

say.text: Pulmonary stenosis sounds like a valve problem, so valvular feels natural. But the component is infundibular (sub-pulmonary).
That narrowing is why most blood shunts toward the aorta.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: the obstruction is below the valve, in the infundibulum.

say.text: Box three: what the ECG and the film show. No hints on this one.
Which line goes in?

choices.label: Left axis deviation with LVH, and plethoric lung fields
Right axis deviation, prominent R in V1, and oligaemic lung fields
Right axis deviation, but a big heart with increased pulmonary markings

say.text: Yes. The ECG shows right axis deviation and prominent R or qR waves in V1, reflecting right atrial enlargement and RVH.
The film can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings, because blood bypasses the lungs.
Left-sided change is tempting because many congenital lesions load the left heart. But TOF loads the right ventricle.
The ECG shows right axis deviation, and the film shows decreased pulmonary vascular markings.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one repays a second look: everything in TOF's ECG points right.

say.text: The right axis is correct, which makes the rest feel safe. But with blood bypassing the lungs, the markings fall instead of rising.
StatPearls describes a normal-size heart silhouette with an upturned apex.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the second half: low pulmonary flow means oligaemia, not plethora.

say.text: Box four: the test ladder. Pick the line that assigns each test its job.

choices.label: Echo is the gold standard; CT shows complex morphology; MRI adds function without radiation
CT is the gold standard for diagnosis, and echo only screens first
Echo, CT and MRI do the same job, so any one will do

say.text: Which test is the first and primary one at the bedside, and what extra question do the other two answer?
Right. Echocardiography is the gold standard and the primary modality, with direct visualisation of the anatomy.
Contrast CT shows the complex morphology; MRI gives anatomy plus function, without ionising radiation.
CT gives striking pictures, which makes it feel like the final word. But echocardiography is the gold standard and stays the primary modality.
CT earns its place by demonstrating the complex cardiovascular morphology.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix it now: the gold standard is echo.

say.text: All three show the heart, so they look interchangeable. But each adds something different.
Echo is primary; CT demonstrates complex morphology; MRI adds functional information without ionising radiation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: the three tests are a ladder, not copies.

say.text: Box five: the spell. Knee-chest positioning goes in the box beside a lever.
Which lever?

choices.label: It increases pulmonary blood flow directly

say.text: Squatting acts on the other side of the resistance balance from oxygen. Which side is oxygen on?
Yes. Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance.
IV phenylephrine pulls the same lever, increasing systemic afterload.
The lungs are short of blood, so a pulmonary lever feels logical. And oxygen does cause pulmonary vasodilation.
Knee-chest is the systemic lever: it increases systemic vascular resistance.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so a second look matters: oxygen is the pulmonary lever, positioning is the systemic one.

say.text: More flow to the lungs is the goal, so it is tempting to think the position delivers it directly. But the position changes systemic resistance.
Pulmonary vasodilation is the job of oxygen.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck: positioning does not touch the lungs directly.

say.text: Box six: the whole spell box. No hints here.
Which version is complete and correct?

choices.label: Oxygen, IV furosemide, an inotrope, fluid restriction, morphine and a vasodilator
Intubate first, then phenylephrine and morphine; positioning and oxygen add little
Knee-chest, oxygen, IV fluid bolus, IV beta-blocker, IV phenylephrine and morphine

say.text: Yes. Each item pulls a lever: knee-chest raises systemic resistance, oxygen causes pulmonary vasodilation, fluid boluses improve RV filling.
IV beta-blockers decrease heart rate and aid RV filling, IV phenylephrine increases systemic afterload, and morphine is a sedative.
A blue, breathless child looks like heart failure, so diuretic and inotrope feel natural. But the spell list works on RV filling and systemic afterload.
A fluid bolus improves RV filling, and phenylephrine increases systemic afterload, so a vasodilator runs the wrong way.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so go back: a spell is not treated like heart failure.

say.text: Spells are urgent, so a big first step feels right. And a rapid, aggressive approach is needed.
But the list itself opens with knee-chest positioning and oxygen, two measures this option drops.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reread: positioning and oxygen are part of the list.

say.text: Box seven: years after repair. The child returns for another operation.
Which reason heads your list?
Look at the valve that the repair has to reconstruct at the outflow tract.
Right. Pulmonary regurgitation results from reconstruction of the RVOT, and pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.
Pulmonary valve replacement can be surgical or transcatheter.
A leftover hole is the classic worry after closing a defect, so it is tempting. But it does not head the list.
Pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so a second look: the commonest reason is the pulmonary valve.

say.text: LV failure sounds serious, so it feels like a late killer. But TOF repair works on the right side.
The most common indication for reoperation is pulmonary insufficiency.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix it: the commonest reoperation reason is pulmonary insufficiency.

say.text: Last box: the legacy line. No hints.
Which line goes in?

choices.label: Arrhythmia, sudden death and endocarditis risks all persist
Repair cures it: no arrhythmia or endocarditis risk follows
Endocarditis matters only before repair; afterwards it is gone

say.text: Yes. Arrhythmias including ventricular tachycardia can occur; 40-50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias.
Sudden death risk is 6-9% 30 years after surgery, and endocarditis risk applies to repaired or unrepaired TOF.
A successful operation feels like a cure, so it is tempting. But the risks continue.
Ventricular arrhythmias can occur in 40-50% of adults with repaired TOF, and sudden death risk is 6-9% at 30 years.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so a second look: repair is not a cure.

say.text: Endocarditis is tied to the defect, so it is tempting to think repair removes it. But the risk applies to repaired or unrepaired TOF.
Arrhythmia and sudden death risks persist as well.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix it: endocarditis risk stays after repair.

say.text: Your take-home so far. Anatomy: VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction, RVH. Blood bypasses the lungs.
ECG: right axis deviation. Film: decreased pulmonary vascular markings. Echo is the gold standard.
Spell levers: knee-chest raises systemic resistance, oxygen dilates the pulmonary bed, fluids improve RV filling.
After repair: pulmonary insufficiency is the commonest reoperation reason; without surgery hypoxic spells cause 68% of deaths.

cards.a: Large anteriorly malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction, RVH.
Infundibular obstruction, blood shunts to the aorta bypassing the lungs, RVH secondary.
Right axis deviation, prominent R in V1; decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
Echocardiography; CT shows complex morphology, MRI adds function without radiation.

cards.q: Lever behind knee-chest and oxygen in a spell?
cards.a: Knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance; oxygen causes pulmonary vasodilation.
